1.d: Name the shift out loud: PLT Lite → PLC Right. This is about student learning, not more meetings.
Highlight where your team is now and circle the shifts you're moving toward.
Use the Alignment sheet to link the three big ideas → four pillars → four critical questions.
Where are we already strong? Where are we still PLT Lite?
Finish the sentence together: "This year, our PLT will focus less on ______ and more on ______."

2.d: Revisit the commitment you wrote in Meeting 1.
Talk about why norms matter when the work gets uncomfortable.

Agree on 4–6 norms written as specific, observable "We will…" commitments (e.g. "We bring scored data to every data meeting"), not vague values like "be respectful." Use the Sample Team Norms and Collective Commitments sheets as models.
Use the Team Roles sheet; decide who takes each role and for how long.

2.t: Make them measurable & set accountability (≈7 min)
2.d: Decide how you'll know you're living each norm, and agree how you'll respond when one is broken. (You'll baseline the broader Collaborative Team Rubric at Meeting 3.)

3.d: Agree up front to be honest without judgment.

Score the Collaborative Team Rubric — frame it as a mirror, not a grade. It stays with the team and isn't reported up. Rate silently first, then compare and reach consensus; expect to be "emerging" in spots — that's a baseline you'll beat. Add the readiness / Critical Issues self-assessment.
Where are you already functioning well? Where are you stuck?
Name one area to grow this cycle — including one rubric descriptor to move up a level by your next check-in.
Decide the course or unit you'll use for this year's learning cycle.

4.d: Revisit anything unclear from Meetings 1–3. This pause is planned, not lost time.
Reaffirm how you work together before the content work begins.
Lock in the course/unit for this cycle.
Brainstorm candidates for the one standard you'll guarantee.
Decide what standards and materials everyone brings next time.

5.d: Re-anchor on the course/unit you chose.
Discuss the difference between what we teach and what students must learn.
Use REAL — readiness, endurance, assessed, leverage — to select just one.
Agree on the single essential standard for this cycle.
Bring student work samples, curriculum, and assessment examples next time.

6.d: Identify the key concepts, skills, vocabulary, and level of rigor.
Turn the standard into smaller, teachable, assessable targets.
Put each target in student-friendly language.
Decide which targets matter most to assess.

7.d: Re-anchor on the learning targets you drafted.
Discuss what proficient student work actually includes.
Create clear criteria for each target.
Look at sample work — do you agree it shows proficiency?
Lock in the success criteria or note what still needs revision.

8.d: Review the essential standard, targets, and success criteria.
Score a sample question, task, or response together — do you agree?
Name any gaps or differences in how you'd score.
Adjust targets or proficiency criteria as needed.
Agree you're ready to design the common assessment.

9.d: Re-anchor on what students must learn and what proficient looks like.

9.t: Decide what counts as evidence (≈10 min)
9.d: What would prove a student learned the target?
Create or select common items and tasks.
Does each item match a learning target?
Divide any item-writing before next time.

10.d: Look at the assessment as a team.
Use the ACID test — check each item against its target.
How will everyone score it the same way?
Decide how you'll record results by student and by target.
Choose the assessment window and the data-review date.

11.d: Re-anchor on what you're teaching toward.
Swap instructional approaches for each target.
Name likely misconceptions and prerequisite skills.
How will you check learning before the CFA?
Lock the teaching window and the CFA date.

12.d: Bring early evidence of student understanding.
What are students getting wrong so far?
Change instruction while there's still time to help.
Nail down when and how you'll give it.
Decide what each teacher brings after the CFA.

13.d: Remind everyone: data is evidence, not judgment.
Look target-by-target, not just at total scores.
Group into proficient, not-yet-proficient, and ready-for-extension.
Compare across classes — what seemed to work?
Choose the target to focus intervention and extension on.

14.d: Re-anchor on what the data showed.
Which strategies produced the strongest results?
What will you replicate, revise, or stop?
Record the team's learning before planning intervention.

15.d: Re-anchor on the target you're responding to.
Build a reteach plan for students who aren't yet proficient.
Design deeper work for students who are ready.
Who provides support, when, and what students will do.
Decide how and when you'll check again.

16.d: How did intervention and extension actually go?
Look at student participation and progress.
Tweak the plan where it isn't working — missteps are expected.
Decide what to bring next time.

17.d: Bring the results from your reassessment.
Identify students who grew and those who still need support.
Which intervention/extension strategies made the difference?
Decide any remaining support for students not yet there.
What did the full cycle teach you?

18.d: Walk from essential standard all the way to reassessment.
Use the Learning Team Quarterly Reflection.
What worked, what was hard, and what to change next year.

18.t: Pick one thing to strengthen (≈5 min)
18.d: Choose one PLC practice to grow in your next cycle.
You completed an authentic cycle. Acknowledge it together.
